title: III. The Medical Experts And A Pound Of Nuts
paragraphs: The medical experts did the prisoner little good either. It came out later that Fetyukovitch had never counted on them much. He had taken up the medical line of defense only because Katerina Ivanovna insisted. She had sent to Moscow for a celebrated doctor for exactly this purpose. The defense could lose nothing by it, of course, and with luck might gain something. Still, the whole thing had a touch of comedy, because the doctors disagreed. The experts were the famous doctor from Moscow, our own Doctor Herzenstube, and the young Doctor Varvinsky. The last two were also witnesses for the prosecution.

Doctor Herzenstube was the first to be called as an expert. He was a gray, bald old man of seventy, of middle height and sturdy build. Everyone in town esteemed and respected him. He was a conscientious doctor and an excellent, pious man, a Hernguter or a Moravian brother, I am not sure which. He had lived among us for many years and carried himself with wonderful dignity. He was kind and humane. He treated the poor and the peasants for nothing, went to see them in their slums and huts, and left money behind for medicine. But he was as stubborn as a mule. Once an idea was in his head, nothing could shake it out. Almost everyone in town knew, by the way, that within two or three days of arriving, the famous doctor had made some extremely insulting remarks about Doctor Herzenstube’s qualifications. The Moscow doctor charged twenty-five roubles a visit. Even so, several people in town were glad of his arrival and rushed to consult him, whatever it cost. All of these had been Doctor Herzenstube’s patients, of course, and the celebrated doctor had criticized his treatment with extreme harshness. In the end, the moment he saw each patient he asked, “Well, who has been stuffing you with quack medicines? Herzenstube? He, he!” Doctor Herzenstube heard all this, naturally. And now all three doctors came forward one after another to be examined.

Doctor Herzenstube declared flatly that the prisoner’s mind was obviously abnormal. He gave his grounds for this opinion, which I leave out here, and added that the abnormality showed not only in many of the prisoner’s past actions but was plain even now, at this very moment. Asked to explain how it was plain at this very moment, the old doctor answered with simple-hearted directness. He said that the prisoner had come into court with “an extraordinary air, remarkable in the circumstances.” He had “marched in like a soldier, looking straight before him, though it would have been more natural for him to look to the left, where the ladies were sitting among the public. He was a great admirer of the fair sex, and he must be thinking a lot about what the ladies are saying of him now.” That is how the old man put it, in his peculiar language.

I must add that he spoke Russian fluently, but he built every sentence the German way. This never bothered him, because it was his weakness to believe he spoke Russian perfectly, better even than Russians do. He was also very fond of Russian proverbs, and always declared they were the best and most expressive sayings in the world. I may mention, too, that in conversation he often forgot the most ordinary words. Through absent-mindedness they would simply go out of his head, though he knew them perfectly well. The same thing happened when he spoke German. At such moments he always waved his hand in front of his face, as if trying to catch the lost word, and nobody could make him go on talking until he had found it. His remark that the prisoner ought to have looked at the ladies when he came in set off a whisper of amusement in the audience. All our ladies were very fond of the old doctor. They also knew that he had been a bachelor all his life, a religious man of exemplary conduct, who looked on women as lofty creatures. So his unexpected remark struck everyone as very odd.

Next the Moscow doctor was questioned. He repeated, firmly and emphatically, that he thought the prisoner’s mental condition abnormal in the highest degree. He spoke at length and learnedly about “aberration” and “mania.” From all the facts collected, he argued, the prisoner had certainly been in a state of aberration for several days before his arrest. If he had committed the crime, then even if he was aware of it, it must have been almost involuntary, since he had no power to control the morbid impulse that possessed him.

But besides temporary aberration, the doctor diagnosed mania, which, he said, promised to lead to complete insanity in the future. (I should note that I am giving this in my own words; the doctor used very learned, professional language.) “All his actions go against common sense and logic,” he continued. “I will not mention what I have not seen, that is, the crime itself and the whole catastrophe. But the day before yesterday, while he was talking to me, he had an unaccountably fixed look in his eye. He laughed suddenly when there was nothing to laugh at. He was constantly and inexplicably irritable, and used strange words, ‘Bernard!’ ‘Ethics!’ and others equally out of place.” But the doctor saw mania above all in the fact that the prisoner could not speak even of the three thousand roubles, which he considered himself cheated of, without extraordinary irritation. Yet he could talk fairly lightly about his other misfortunes and grievances. By all accounts, whenever the three thousand roubles came up in the past, he had flown into a perfect frenzy. And yet he was said to be a disinterested man, not a grasping one.

“As for the opinion of my learned colleague,” the Moscow doctor added ironically at the end, “that the prisoner would naturally have looked at the ladies when he came into court, and not straight ahead, I will say only this. Quite apart from the playfulness of the theory, it is radically unsound. I fully agree that the prisoner, entering the court where his fate will be decided, would not naturally stare straight ahead in that fixed way, and that this may really be a sign of his abnormal mental condition. But at the same time I maintain that he would naturally not look to the left at the ladies. He would look, on the contrary, to the right, to find his legal adviser, on whose help all his hopes rest and on whose defense his whole future depends.” The doctor gave his opinion positively and emphatically.

But then Doctor Varvinsky’s unexpected pronouncement put the last touch of comedy on the experts’ disagreement. In his opinion the prisoner was now, and had been all along, in a perfectly normal condition. Before his arrest he must certainly have been nervous and exceedingly excited, but there were several perfectly obvious causes for that: jealousy, anger, constant drunkenness, and so on. This nervous state, though, did not involve the mental aberration just mentioned. As for whether the prisoner should have looked to the left or to the right on entering the court, “in his modest opinion” the prisoner would naturally look straight ahead, as he had in fact done, because that was where the judges, who held his fate in their hands, were sitting. So it was exactly by looking straight ahead that he showed his perfectly normal state of mind at present. The young doctor finished his “modest” testimony rather heatedly.
“Bravo, doctor!” Mitya cried from his seat. “Just so!”

Mitya was reprimanded, of course. But the young doctor’s opinion had a decisive effect on the judges and the public, and, as it turned out later, everyone agreed with him. Doctor Herzenstube, though, was quite unexpectedly useful to Mitya when he was called as a witness. As an old resident of the town who had known the Karamazov family for years, he supplied some facts of great value to the prosecution. Then suddenly, as if remembering something, he added:

“But the poor young man might have had a very different life, for he had a good heart as a child and after childhood, that I know. But the Russian proverb says, ‘If a man has one head, it’s good, but if another clever man comes to visit him, it would be better still, for then there will be two heads and not only one.’”

“One head is good, but two are better,” the prosecutor put in impatiently. He knew the old man’s habit of talking slowly and deliberately, with no regard for the impression he was making or the delay he was causing. He also knew how highly the old man valued his flat, dull, always gleefully self-satisfied German wit. The old man loved to make jokes.

“Oh, yes, that’s what I say,” he went on obstinately. “One head is good, but two are much better, but he did not meet another head with wits, and his wits went. Where did they go? I’ve forgotten the word.” He passed his hand before his eyes and went on, “Oh, yes, _spazieren_.”
“Wandering?”

“Oh, yes, wandering, that’s what I say. Well, his wits went wandering and fell in a hole so deep that he lost himself. And yet he was a grateful and feeling boy. Oh, I remember him very well, a little chap so high, left neglected by his father in the back yard, running about with no boots on his feet and his little breeches hanging by one button.”
A note of feeling and tenderness suddenly came into the honest old man’s voice. Fetyukovitch gave a positive start, like a man who scents something, and caught at it at once.

“Oh, yes, I was a young man then.... I was ... well, I was forty-five then, and had only just come here. And I was so sorry for the boy then. I asked myself why shouldn’t I buy him a pound of ... a pound of what? I’ve forgotten what it’s called. A pound of what children are very fond of, what is it, what is it?” The doctor began waving his hands again. “It grows on a tree and is gathered and given to everybody....”
“Apples?”
“Oh, no, no. You have a dozen apples, not a pound.... No, there are a lot of them, and all little. You put them in the mouth and crack.”
“Nuts?”

“Quite so, nuts, I say so.” The doctor repeated it in the calmest way, as though he had never been at a loss for the word. “And I bought him a pound of nuts, for no one had ever bought the boy a pound of nuts before. And I lifted my finger and said to him, ‘Boy, _Gott der Vater_.’ He laughed and said, ‘_Gott der Vater_.’... ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ He laughed again and lisped, ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ Then he laughed and said as best he could, ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ I went away, and two days after I happened to be passing, and he shouted to me of his own accord, ‘Uncle, _Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_,’ and he had only forgotten ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ But I reminded him of it, and I felt very sorry for him again. But he was taken away, and I did not see him again. Twenty-three years passed. I am sitting one morning in my study, a white-haired old man, when there walks into the room a blooming young man I should never have known, but he held up his finger and said, laughing, ‘_Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_, and _Gott der heilige Geist_. I have just arrived and have come to thank you for that pound of nuts, for no one else ever bought me a pound of nuts; you are the only one that ever did.’ And then I remembered my happy youth and the poor child in the yard, with no boots on his feet, and my heart was touched and I said, ‘You are a grateful young man, for you have remembered all your life the pound of nuts I bought you in your childhood.’ And I embraced him and blessed him. And I shed tears. He laughed, but he shed tears, too ... for the Russian often laughs when he ought to be weeping. But he did weep; I saw it. And now, alas!...”
“And I am weeping now too, German, I am weeping now, you saintly man,” Mitya cried suddenly.

At any rate, the anecdote made a certain favorable impression on the public. But the chief sensation in Mitya’s favor was caused by Katerina Ivanovna’s evidence, which I will describe in a moment. In fact, once the witnesses _à décharge_, that is, those called by the defense, began to testify, fortune seemed all at once markedly kinder to Mitya. What was particularly striking was that this surprised even the counsel for the defense. But before Katerina Ivanovna was called, Alyosha was examined. He recalled a fact that seemed to furnish positive evidence against one important point made by the prosecution.
